influenza-selection-timing.title: Match Drug to Patient and Setting
influenza-selection-timing.summary: Treat priority patients promptly, interpret the two-day window in context, and match the antiviral to setting, age, route and evidence limits.
influenza-selection-timing.application: Choose an antiviral from the patient’s treatment priority, setting and delivery needs; verify product-specific eligibility, safety and interactions before selecting for convenience.

lesson.heading: Use time and priority together
lesson.body: Benefit is greatest when treatment starts early, ideally within two days of symptom onset. The book and CDC support prompt treatment for hospitalized patients, severe or progressive illness, and patients at higher risk of complications even when more than 48 hours have passed. Do not delay treatment in these priority groups while awaiting influenza test results. For an otherwise healthy outpatient without higher-risk features, CDC permits consideration of early treatment based on clinical judgment when it can start within two days; this is not a requirement to treat every uncomplicated illness.

lesson.heading: Prefer oseltamivir in hospitalized influenza
lesson.body: CDC recommends oral or enterically administered oseltamivir as soon as possible for hospitalized patients with suspected or confirmed influenza, including those presenting after two days. Inhaled zanamivir, IV peramivir and oral baloxavir are not routinely recommended for hospitalized influenza because evidence of clinical benefit is insufficient. A single-dose outpatient indication or an IV route does not establish a preferred hospital regimen. These hospital recommendations draw on evidence beyond the acute uncomplicated influenza indications in FDA labeling.

lesson.heading: Assess an unreliable enteral route
lesson.body: Hospitalization or a feeding tube alone does not mean oseltamivir cannot be delivered or absorbed. Evaluate actual enteral tolerance and absorption. CDC states that IV peramivir may be considered when a hospitalized patient cannot tolerate or absorb oral or enteric oseltamivir, such as with gastric stasis, malabsorption or gastrointestinal bleeding. This is a qualified alternative, not proof of routine inpatient efficacy: the Rapivab label states that efficacy could not be established in serious influenza requiring hospitalization. Review renal function and the clinical context rather than automatically substituting a single outpatient dose.

lesson.heading: Verify treatment age and route
lesson.body: For eligible uncomplicated outpatients presenting within two days, CDC lists oral oseltamivir, inhaled zanamivir, IV peramivir and oral baloxavir. Verify each product: FDA treatment ages are at least two weeks for oseltamivir, seven years for zanamivir, six months for peramivir and five years for baloxavir. CDC and AAP also recommend oseltamivir treatment in younger infants outside that labeled age. Treatment ages differ from prophylaxis ages. Zanamivir requires correct Diskhaler use and is not recommended with underlying airway disease because of serious bronchospasm risk; milk-protein allergy is a labeled contraindication. Check renal dosing needs for oseltamivir and peramivir and verify the specific formulation, weight-based dose and access.

lesson.heading: Respect baloxavir population limits
lesson.body: The current Xofluza label permits treatment of acute uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours in patients at least five years old who are otherwise healthy or at high risk of complications. CDC does not recommend baloxavir during pregnancy or breastfeeding because relevant human efficacy and safety data are unavailable; oral oseltamivir is the preferred influenza treatment during pregnancy. CDC also does not recommend baloxavir monotherapy in severely immunosuppressed patients, where prolonged replication raises resistance concerns. Do not broaden that wording to every immune condition or assume its outpatient high-risk indication establishes efficacy for hospitalized or complicated/progressive illness. These evidence-based recommendations are distinct from the label’s hypersensitivity contraindication.

lesson.heading: Make delivery part of selection
lesson.body: A convenient schedule cannot overcome poor delivery, an unsuitable population or a clinically important interaction. Relenza is a dry powder for oral inhalation through the supplied Diskhaler, not a powder to place in a nebulizer or ventilator. Assess the patient’s ability to use the device and provide instruction. Xofluza has oral suspension presentations for swallowing difficulty or enteral administration; follow the instructions for the actual presentation. Avoid taking baloxavir with dairy products, calcium-fortified beverages, or polyvalent-cation-containing antacids, laxatives or oral supplements because these can reduce exposure. Availability of a suspension or feeding-tube route does not change its population or illness-setting limits.

keyPoints: Start priority patients promptly; more than 48 hours does not rule out treatment.
Oral or enteric oseltamivir is the routine hospitalized choice.
Verify product-specific age, delivery, safety and renal dosing requirements.
Baloxavir convenience does not overcome its evidence limits or cation interactions.

check.question: What routine antiviral does CDC recommend for hospitalized influenza?
choices: Oral or enterically administered oseltamivir
Single-dose baloxavir
Inhaled zanamivir for every patient
No therapy after 48 hours
check.rationale: CDC recommends oral or enterically administered oseltamivir promptly for hospitalized influenza, including presentation after 48 hours. Baloxavir and inhaled zanamivir are not routine hospitalized choices; zanamivir also requires airway and device suitability. The two-day window is not a reason to withhold treatment from a hospitalized patient.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-033.question: A patient hospitalized with suspected influenza presents four days after symptoms began. What should the timing decision be?
choices: Start recommended antiviral treatment promptly rather than applying a universal 48-hour cutoff
Withhold all influenza antivirals because two days have passed
Delay treatment until symptoms have lasted seven days
Treat only if the patient was not vaccinated
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-033.rationale: Hospitalized influenza is a treatment-priority condition even after two days. There is no seven-day waiting requirement, and vaccination history does not remove the treatment indication.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-034.question: An otherwise healthy outpatient without higher-risk features has uncomplicated influenza symptoms for one day. How does CDC frame antiviral treatment?
choices: It may be considered on clinical judgment when it can start within two days
It is mandatory for every uncomplicated illness regardless of clinical judgment
It should be delayed until the third day
It requires hospitalization before it can be considered
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-034.rationale: CDC allows early treatment consideration in non-high-risk outpatients based on clinical judgment. It does not require universal treatment, delayed initiation or admission.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-035.question: A high-risk outpatient has suspected influenza and treatment is indicated. Which action best reflects CDC treatment priority?
choices: Begin treatment promptly without waiting for influenza laboratory confirmation
Wait for laboratory confirmation before any treatment in every case
Wait until the patient becomes hospitalized
Withhold treatment solely because symptoms exceed 48 hours
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-035.rationale: Priority patients should be treated promptly without awaiting test confirmation. Hospitalization is not required, and elapsed time beyond two days alone does not exclude treatment of high-risk patients.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-036.question: Which interpretation of the early influenza treatment window should be corrected?
choices: The greatest benefit within two days means no patient can benefit from later treatment
Early treatment generally provides the greatest benefit
Hospitalized patients should still receive recommended treatment after two days
Timing must be interpreted with severity and risk of complications
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-036.rationale: An early-benefit window is not a universal exclusion rule. Early treatment is preferable, but hospital, severity and high-risk context support later treatment.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-037.question: Which regimen is CDC’s routine preferred antiviral approach for a hospitalized patient with suspected influenza?
choices: Oral or enterically administered oseltamivir started promptly
Single-dose baloxavir chosen solely for convenience
Inhaled zanamivir regardless of airway disease or device ability
IV peramivir for every admission because intravenous delivery proves superior benefit
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-037.rationale: CDC recommends oral or enteric oseltamivir for hospitalized influenza. Baloxavir, zanamivir and peramivir are not routinely recommended there because clinical-benefit evidence is insufficient; convenience or an IV route does not establish superiority.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-038.question: Why are baloxavir, inhaled zanamivir and IV peramivir not routinely recommended for hospitalized influenza?
choices: Evidence of clinical benefit in hospitalized patients is insufficient
All three are FDA contraindicated in every hospitalized patient
All three have no antiviral activity against influenza
Every hospitalized patient is unable to absorb oseltamivir
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-038.rationale: CDC cites insufficient hospitalized clinical-benefit evidence, not universal FDA contraindications or lack of antiviral activity. Hospitalization alone does not establish failed enteral absorption.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-039.question: A hospitalized patient has gastric stasis and cannot absorb enteric oseltamivir. Which statement fits CDC guidance?
choices: IV peramivir may be considered as a qualified alternative after clinical and renal assessment
Peramivir is proven superior for all hospitalized influenza
Use a single outpatient peramivir dose without assessing the hospitalized illness
Replace oseltamivir with baloxavir solely because both have oral suspension options
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-039.rationale: CDC allows consideration of IV peramivir when oral or enteric oseltamivir cannot be tolerated or absorbed. Inpatient benefit is not established generally, an outpatient regimen cannot be automatically transferred, and a baloxavir suspension does not solve a setting-evidence problem.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-040.question: A hospitalized patient receives medications through a functioning feeding tube and has no identified malabsorption. Which inference should be corrected?
choices: A feeding tube alone proves oseltamivir cannot be absorbed and requires routine peramivir
Enteric oseltamivir remains CDC’s routine hospitalized option
Delivery and absorption should be assessed individually
An IV route alone does not prove better clinical benefit
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-040.rationale: A functioning tube does not by itself establish failed enteral delivery or absorption. Individual assessment and the routine enteric oseltamivir recommendation remain appropriate; intravenous delivery alone is not superiority evidence.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-041.question: Which age statement correctly describes the FDA treatment indication for inhaled zanamivir?
choices: Acute uncomplicated influenza treatment is indicated from seven years of age; the prophylaxis age differs
Its treatment indication begins at five years because that is its prophylaxis age
Its treatment indication begins at six months because peramivir is approved then
There is no need to check age for an inhaled antiviral
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-041.rationale: Relenza treatment begins at seven years; prophylaxis begins at five years. Peramivir’s six-month treatment age cannot be applied to zanamivir, and age must be verified.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-042.question: An outpatient with asthma is being considered for influenza therapy. What is the appropriate interpretation of inhaled zanamivir?
choices: It is not recommended with underlying airway disease because of serious bronchospasm risk
It is preferred because all inhaled medicines improve asthma
Its dry powder should be mixed into a nebulizer to eliminate risk
Only milk-protein allergy matters; airway disease can be ignored
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-042.rationale: The book, CDC and Relenza labeling identify bronchospasm risk with underlying airway disease. Inhalation does not imply asthma benefit; the supplied powder must not be nebulized. Milk-protein allergy is a separate contraindication and does not replace airway assessment.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-043.question: Which statement correctly separates oseltamivir’s FDA treatment age from CDC/AAP recommendations?
choices: FDA labeling begins at two weeks, while CDC/AAP also recommend treatment in younger infants
FDA labeling begins at one year because that is the prophylaxis age
CDC prohibits treatment in all infants younger than two weeks
The baloxavir five-year age can be applied to oseltamivir
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-043.rationale: Tamiflu labeling permits treatment from two weeks, with younger-infant treatment recommended by CDC/AAP outside that labeled age. Prophylaxis and other-drug ages cannot be substituted.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-044.question: An eligible outpatient is considering baloxavir while taking an oral calcium supplement. What should be addressed?
choices: Avoid concomitant use with polyvalent-cation-containing supplements and verify the product-specific dose and presentation
Take the supplement with baloxavir to improve absorption
Use a dairy beverage to avoid the cation interaction
Assume one-dose convenience removes the need to review interactions
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-044.rationale: Xofluza labeling advises avoiding concomitant polyvalent cations because exposure can be reduced. Dairy and calcium-fortified beverages are also included; a single dose still requires interaction and formulation review.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-045.question: Which immune-host statement accurately reflects CDC’s baloxavir monotherapy recommendation?
choices: It is not recommended in severely immunosuppressed patients because prolonged replication raises resistance concern
It is prohibited for every patient with any immune condition regardless of severity
It is preferred in severe immunosuppression solely because it is one dose
Its uncomplicated high-risk indication proves efficacy for every immunosuppressed hospitalized patient
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-045.rationale: CDC specifies severely immunosuppressed patients for this monotherapy recommendation. Do not broaden it to every immune condition or infer universal severe-host inpatient benefit from convenience or an outpatient high-risk indication.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-046.question: Why does CDC not recommend baloxavir during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
choices: Relevant human efficacy and safety data are unavailable; this recommendation is distinct from the label’s hypersensitivity contraindication
The FDA label lists pregnancy as an absolute hypersensitivity contraindication
Animal data alone establish proven human safety in both settings
Being oral makes baloxavir the preferred treatment in pregnancy
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-046.rationale: CDC cites unavailable relevant human data. The labeled contraindication concerns hypersensitivity, and animal results do not establish human pregnancy or lactation safety. Oral oseltamivir is preferred during pregnancy.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-047.question: Which patient fits the current Xofluza labeled treatment population, subject to the remaining safety and dosing checks?
choices: An otherwise healthy six-year-old with acute uncomplicated influenza beginning yesterday
A four-year-old selected solely because suspension is available
A hospitalized adult with complicated influenza selected solely for a one-dose schedule
An adult with uncomplicated influenza beginning five days ago selected under the within-48-hour label
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-047.rationale: The label permits acute uncomplicated treatment from five years within 48 hours, including otherwise healthy patients. A suspension does not lower the age, and convenience does not extend the labeled setting or symptom window.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-048.question: A patient cannot swallow tablets. Which statement about a baloxavir suspension is correct?
choices: An appropriate suspension presentation may address delivery, but age, illness setting and interactions still must be checked
Suspension availability establishes routine efficacy in hospitalized influenza
Suspension eliminates interactions with calcium products
Every suspension presentation has identical preparation instructions
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-048.rationale: The label provides suspension presentations for swallowing difficulty and enteral administration. Delivery options do not establish hospital efficacy or remove cation interactions, and instructions differ by presentation.

influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-179.question: A hospitalized patient has had symptoms for four days. What routine antiviral does CDC recommend?
choices: Oral or enterically administered oseltamivir
No treatment because 48 hours passed
Single-dose baloxavir
Inhaled zanamivir regardless of airway disease
influenza-antiviral-pharmacology-179.rationale: CDC recommends oral or enterically administered oseltamivir promptly for hospitalized influenza, including four days after symptom onset. The 48-hour window does not exclude treatment here. Baloxavir and inhaled zanamivir are not routine hospitalized choices, and zanamivir also requires assessment of airway disease and device suitability.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Use time and priority together
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: Book early-benefit and later priority treatment preserved; current CDC adds discretionary non-high-risk treatment and no testing delay. Late treatment is not a universal baloxavir eligibility extension.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Prefer oseltamivir in hospitalized influenza
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: Routine oral/enteric oseltamivir, timely late treatment and insufficient routine inpatient evidence verified. Hospital guidance distinguished from uncomplicated FDA indications.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Assess an unreliable enteral route
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: Gastric stasis/malabsorption/GI bleeding are qualified enteral intolerance/absorption contexts. Peramivir may be considered; no universal inpatient efficacy or automatic one-dose regimen inferred.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Verify treatment age and route
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: All four treatment ages and oseltamivir younger-infant guidance checked individually. Treatment/prophylaxis distinction explicit. Milk-protein allergy labeled contraindication separate from underlying-airway nonrecommendation. Renal dose review not a fabricated dose.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Respect baloxavir population limits
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: Five-year uncomplicated <=48-hour healthy/high-risk label verified. CDC severe immunosuppression qualification retained, human pregnancy/lactation data limits distinguished from hypersensitivity contraindication. Animal data not human safety proof.

wholeBodyComparison.heading: Make delivery part of selection
wholeBodyComparison.comparison: Device-only dry-powder route and no nebulization/ventilation verified. Actual suspension presentations support enteral delivery; cation/dairy interaction retained without inventing separation intervals. Delivery does not change illness/population evidence.

No treatment because 48 hours passed
